questions.prompt: Per this course's additive-only rule, which of these correctly describes how organization-wide defaults (OWD) relate to every other sharing mechanism covered in this course?
options: OWD sets a baseline that every other mechanism can only widen, never narrow — a sharing rule, team, or manual share can grant more access than OWD, but none of them can take access away
OWD is simply the default access level shown in list views; actual security is controlled entirely by sharing rules
OWD only applies to custom objects; standard objects always default to Public Read/Write
OWD can be overridden downward by any sharing rule that specifies a lower access level
questions.distractorExplain: Option D is the common misconception: if OWD already grants broad access, there is no declarative sharing rule that can subtract from it — Restriction Rules exist specifically because no sharing rule can do this.
questions.explain: Every mechanism in this course — role hierarchy, sharing rules, teams, manual sharing, Apex managed sharing, territories — is additive on top of OWD. Only a Restriction Rule, covered as the one deliberate exception, removes access rather than granting it.

questions.prompt: An admin is designing a 1,200-person org's role hierarchy and is tempted to create one role for every title on the official org chart, mirroring middle management exactly. Per this course's guidance, what's the main risk of that approach?
options: It's technically impossible — Salesforce hard-caps the number of roles at 50
Every added level increases sharing-recalculation scope and administrative overhead, often without matching the org's real visibility needs
Role hierarchies cannot contain more than one branch, so departments must share a single role
Public Read/Write objects are required once a role hierarchy exceeds five levels
questions.explain: Depth has a real computational and administrative cost — each added level widens the scope of what has to be recalculated when roles change, and mirroring every title rarely matches the actual visibility requirements. The guidance is wide-and-shallow, not one role per title.

questions.prompt: An object's OWD is Private. A record owner clicks the Sharing button and manually shares the record with a colleague at Read Only. The record's ownership is later transferred to a different user. What happens to that manual share?
options: It transfers automatically so the new owner's manual shares stack on top of it
It is converted into a sharing rule automatically
It is automatically removed, because manual shares are tied to the ownership context they were created under
It stays in force permanently regardless of ownership changes
questions.explain: Salesforce automatically removes a manual share when the record's owner changes, since the grant no longer makes sense once ownership shifts — this is deliberate cleanup behavior, not a bug.

questions.prompt: A Support Escalations team needs visibility into every Case marked Priority = Critical, no matter which agent owns it. Which kind of sharing rule fits, and why?
options: An owner-based sharing rule, because ownership determines the escalations team's interest
Manual sharing, because the requirement is one-off
A change to organization-wide defaults, since that's the only way to affect every Case
A criteria-based sharing rule, because the requirement depends on a field value on the record, independent of who owns it
questions.explain: Because visibility depends on a field value (Priority = Critical) rather than ownership, a criteria-based sharing rule is the correct tool — it re-evaluates whenever a qualifying field changes, regardless of who owns the record.

questions.prompt: Match each organization-wide default setting to what it actually controls.
right: Only the owner (and anyone above them in the role hierarchy) can see the record
Everyone in the org can see every record, but only the owner (and above) can edit it
Everyone in the org can see and edit every record by default
A detail record's visibility exactly mirrors its master-detail parent's visibility
questions.explain: Private restricts to owner (and hierarchy above); Public Read Only lets everyone see but only the owner (and above) edit; Public Read/Write lets everyone see and edit; Controlled by Parent exactly mirrors the master-detail parent's visibility with no independent setting of its own.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: a sharing grant made through the Sharing button on a record carries a RowCause value of ________ on that object's companion Share object.
questions.explain: Manual sharing writes a Share-object row with RowCause = 'Manual', distinguishing it from rows generated by a role, a sharing rule, a team, or a custom Apex sharing reason.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about Account Teams and Opportunity Teams, per this course.
options: A team attaches a list of people to one specific record, each with an individual access level and team role on that record
A default team is a user-level template that gets copied onto every new record that user creates going forward
Changing your default team retroactively updates the team already sitting on records you created last month
Teams trigger the same asynchronous sharing recalculation job that sharing rules do
If the same five-person team needs to be added to every record a given owner creates, that's a signal the requirement has outgrown teams and belongs in a sharing rule or role-hierarchy change
questions.explain: Teams attach to one record at a time with individual access levels (true), and a default team is only a template copied at creation time, so changing it later never retroactively updates existing records (option 2 is false) — and because team membership is just data on the record, there's no recalculation job to trigger (option 3 is false). A team applied identically and repeatedly to every record from one owner is really a population-level sharing requirement in disguise.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about public groups and queues, per this course.
options: A public group grants nothing by itself — it only matters once a sharing rule, manual share, or other mechanism targets it
A public group nested inside another public group expands the outer group's effective membership transitively, which is a known audit risk
Every member of a queue automatically has access to every record currently assigned to that queue, simply by being a member
Once a record is taken out of a queue by an individual owner, the other former queue members keep their implicit access permanently
questions.explain: A public group has no effect until targeted by something else (true); nesting expands effective membership invisibly, which is why it's an audit risk (true); queue membership grants implicit access to everything currently in the queue (true). Implicit queue access disappears once a record leaves the queue for an individual owner — it is not retained, which makes option 3 false.

questions.prompt: What does the RowCause field on a sharing row (such as an OpportunityShare row, or a custom object's __Share row) record?
options: The access level — Read or Edit — granted by that row
The reason the row exists — for example Owner, Manual, a sharing rule, or a custom Apex sharing reason
The date the share row was created
Which user or group receives the access
questions.distractorExplain: Option A describes AccessLevel, not RowCause — AccessLevel records what access (Read/Edit) is granted, while RowCause records why the row exists at all. The two fields answer different questions about the same grant.
questions.explain: RowCause is the field that explains why a given share row exists — distinguishing an owner-implied row, a manual share, a sharing-rule-generated row, and a custom Apex-defined reason from each other.

questions.prompt: A record's owner changes. What happens differently to a manual share versus an Apex managed share that were both already on that record?
options: The manual share is automatically removed; the Apex managed share persists until code explicitly removes it
Both are automatically removed, since both are tied to the previous owner
The Apex managed share is automatically removed; the manual share persists
Neither is affected by an ownership change
questions.explain: Manual sharing is cleared automatically on an ownership change because the platform assumes it may no longer apply. Apex managed sharing deliberately does not get cleared — it's meant to represent a durable business fact that survives reassignment, until the code that created it removes it.

questions.prompt: An admin builds a technically correct Sharing Set access mapping for Customer Community Users on the Case object, but a portal user still sees zero cases. What is the most likely cause, per this course?
options: Sharing Sets cannot be applied to the Case object under any configuration
The org-wide default for Case needs to be raised to Public Read/Write first
A second Sharing Set must always be layered on top of the first
The Customer Community User profile itself was never given object-level Read access to Case, so the Sharing Set has nothing to add on top of
questions.explain: A Sharing Set only adds access on top of what the external user's profile already permits. If the profile itself lacks object-level access, the access mapping is irrelevant — this is the single most common first-time Sharing Set misconfiguration.

questions.prompt: Match each Enterprise Territory Management building block to what it actually is.
right: The org-wide, one-way switch that turns Enterprise Territory Management on
A category every territory must belong to, carrying a priority for overlapping access paths
The container for one complete territory hierarchy; only one can be Active org-wide
An individual node in a model's hierarchy, with its own user/account assignments and access-level overrides
questions.explain: Territory Settings is the one-way org-wide activation switch. Territory Type is the category every territory belongs to, carrying priority. Territory Model is the container holding one full hierarchy, with only one Active at a time. Territory is the individual node inside a model's hierarchy, with its own assignments and overrides.

questions.prompt: Match each mechanism to the one statement that correctly describes it.
right: Grants external (high-volume) users access based on their profile, mapped through a lookup relationship on the record
The role-based equivalent used for partner/role-structured external licenses, targeting groups, roles, or roles-and-subordinates instead of profiles
Removes visibility to matching records for matching users, on top of whatever access they'd otherwise have
Narrows the default record set shown in list views/reports/SOQL without changing a user's actual sharing access
questions.explain: Sharing Sets grant profile-based external access via a lookup mapping. Share Groups are the role-based equivalent for role-structured external licenses. Restriction Rules remove visibility on top of whatever access a user would otherwise have. Scoping Rules only narrow the default view shown, without touching actual access.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: as of this course's writing, defining a custom Apex sharing reason on a custom object is only exposed in Salesforce ________ (or via the Metadata/Tooling API) — there is no Lightning Experience screen for it.
questions.explain: Apex Sharing Reasons are configured from the custom object's detail page in Salesforce Classic, or created headlessly via the Metadata/Tooling API — a build checklist assuming everything is in Lightning will stall here.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about implicit sharing, per this course.
options: If a user has access to an Opportunity through any mechanism, they automatically get read-only access to that Opportunity's parent Account, even with no explicit grant on the Account itself
Implicit sharing is configured from its own dedicated Setup page, the same way sharing rules are
Child sharing can extend Account access down to related Contacts, Opportunities, and Cases, depending on the Account owner's role's child access settings
An access audit that only checks sharing rules, teams, and manual shares risks under-reporting who can actually see a record
questions.explain: Parent sharing grants read-only parent visibility automatically (true). Child sharing can extend Account access to children based on the owner's role child-access settings (true). Because implicit sharing has no dedicated Setup page and isn't a configured rule (option 1 is false), an audit limited to explicit mechanisms can easily under-report real access (true).

questions.prompt: An architect reviews an object and finds twelve separate criteria-based sharing rules, each covering a slightly different narrow exception. What does this pattern most often indicate, per this course's layered model?
options: The object correctly needed twelve distinct exceptions, and no redesign is warranted
Apex managed sharing should be added as a thirteenth mechanism
The OWD or role hierarchy baseline for that object was likely set incorrectly to begin with, pushing work onto the exception layer that belongs one layer up
Restriction Rules should replace all twelve sharing rules
questions.explain: A pile of narrow exceptions is usually a symptom that the baseline (OWD or role hierarchy) doesn't match the real access pattern, not evidence the business genuinely needed that many bespoke rules.

questions.prompt: Why can a Public Read/Write OWD actually outperform a Private OWD on the same high-volume object, even though it grants more access by default?
options: Public Read/Write disables the role hierarchy entirely, so there's less to compute
With Public Read/Write, no sharing rows beyond the owner are needed at all, since nothing beyond the default needs representing — Private generates rows that must be stored, indexed, and recalculated
Public Read/Write records are stored in a separate, faster database table
Private OWD always disables indexing on the object
questions.explain: The moment OWD is Private or Public Read Only, every grant beyond the owner becomes a sharing row that must be maintained. If OWD is already the most open setting, there's nothing extra to store or recalculate — which is why sharing-row count, not raw record count, usually drives performance at scale.

questions.prompt: A support ticket says a field was added to a page layout, but a specific profile still can't see it on the record page, with no error shown. What's the most likely cause, and where would you check first?
options: The record's OWD is set to Private; check the Sharing Settings page
The page layout itself was deleted; check Object Manager's layout list
The user lacks the 'View All' object permission; check their permission set assignments
Field-level security hides the field for that profile; check View Field Accessibility, not the page layout editor
questions.explain: This is the classic FLS-versus-layout trap: being on the layout only controls arrangement, not visibility. FLS silently hides a field with no error, so View Field Accessibility — not the layout editor — is the fastest way to confirm it.

questions.prompt: Match each type of data skew to its description.
right: Thousands of child records sitting under a single Account, which can stall bulk DML and data loads
One user or queue owning a very large number of records under a restrictive sharing model, which can trigger a massive recalculation on an upstream hierarchy change
A large number of records pointing at the same target record through a plain lookup field, causing locking and contention on writes to that target
questions.explain: Account data skew concentrates children under one parent Account. Ownership skew concentrates records under one owner, making upstream hierarchy changes trigger outsized recalculation. Lookup skew concentrates records pointing at one shared target through a plain lookup field, causing contention on that target.

questions.prompt: Match each design decision to the case-study requirement it was built to satisfy.
left: A Restriction Rule carving out Under_Regulatory_Review__c records
Separate Private Banking and Retail Advisory role-hierarchy branches
Enterprise Territory Management as the structural backbone
A criteria-based sharing rule for Named Account Managers
right: Meridian Wealth Partners — a hard legal requirement to hide flagged households from everyone except Compliance and the advisor of record
Meridian Wealth Partners — structurally guaranteeing Retail Advisors can never see Private Banking households
Orbis Industrial — access genuinely follows territory assignment rather than a management reporting line
Orbis Industrial — a narrow exception for accounts spanning multiple territories, layered on top of the territory baseline
questions.explain: The Restriction Rule satisfies Meridian's legally-mandated regulatory-review carve-out. The two separate role-hierarchy branches structurally guarantee Meridian's Private Banking / Retail Advisory separation. Territory Management is Orbis's backbone because access follows territory, not a reporting line. The Named Account Manager sharing rule is Orbis's narrow, deliberate exception for accounts spanning multiple territories.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: while Defer Sharing Calculations is active, the sharing table still reflects the pre-deferral state for the affected changes, until an admin explicitly runs ________.
questions.explain: Resume Sharing Calculations is the action that triggers one net recalculation covering everything done during the deferred window, rather than recalculating after every intermediate change.

questions.prompt: Put these steps of a planned, deferred bulk sharing change in the correct order, per this course's recommended pattern.
items: Confirm Defer Sharing Calculations is available and enable it before starting
Make the full batch of role, territory, or group-membership changes
Run Resume Sharing Calculations to trigger one net recalculation
Confirm the recalculation job completes cleanly before reopening access to users
questions.explain: The disciplined pattern is to enable deferral first, make every change in the batch without triggering recalculation after each one, explicitly resume to run a single net recalculation, and verify it completes before treating the new structure as live for users.

questions.prompt: Put these five categories of sharing-design decision in the order this course recommends working through them.
items: Shape role hierarchy and territory hierarchy to match real lines of accountability
Layer sharing rules, teams, and public groups for genuine exceptions
Reserve manual sharing and Apex managed sharing for what the declarative layers can't express
Add restriction rules only if a narrow slice of records must be hidden from what the layers above would otherwise expose
questions.explain: Working in this order — OWD first, then role/territory hierarchy, then declarative exceptions, then manual/Apex sharing, then restriction rules last — prevents picking a convenient OWD and discovering three sharing rules later that the hierarchy should have done the work.

questions.prompt: A user reports they can suddenly see Opportunities they couldn't see last week. Which tool tells you what sharing-model change caused it and when, versus which tool tells you exactly why this user has access to one specific record right now?
options: Setup Audit Trail tells you what changed and when; a record's own sharing detail page tells you exactly who has access to that one record and why
Both questions are answered only by the Background Jobs page
Health Check tells you what changed; Setup Audit Trail tells you why one record is visible
A record's sharing detail page tells you what changed org-wide; Setup Audit Trail tells you about one specific record
questions.explain: Setup Audit Trail answers 'what changed, by whom, and when' at the org level. A record's sharing detail page answers 'why does this specific user see this specific record right now' by listing every user/group with access and the reason. Checking both together avoids relying on just one incomplete answer.

questions.prompt: Per the real Salesforce CTA review board's scoring philosophy as described in this course, which candidate behavior tends to score better?
options: Defending the original design unchanged, even after the panel points out a clear flaw in it
Refusing to answer a 'what if' follow-up question that wasn't part of the original scenario
Openly explaining the trade-offs behind a reasonable design and adapting cleanly when the panel introduces a new constraint
Memorizing one universally correct sharing design and applying it to every scenario
questions.explain: The board's scoring is rubric-based and explicitly not looking for one memorized correct design — a candidate who explains trade-offs honestly and adapts when the panel introduces new constraints typically scores better than one who rigidly defends an original answer after a flaw is pointed out.

questions.prompt: Match each sharing-design trade-off dimension to what it actually measures.
right: How much configuration, Apex, or data-model change the option requires before it's live
Who has to update the design as the business changes, and how often it needs touching
Whether the option triggers frequent, expensive sharing recalculation, and how that scales as data volume grows
Whether a reviewer can see why a user has access by opening Setup, or whether the logic lives inside Apex code only a developer can trace
questions.explain: Build cost is the up-front effort to stand the design up. Maintenance cost is the ongoing effort to keep it correct. Performance and recalculation impact is about how often and how expensively it triggers recalculation at scale. Auditability is about whether access decisions are traceable in Setup versus buried in code.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: the on-screen View Setup Audit Trail page holds only the last ________ entries; a download link pulls the full six months of history as a CSV.
questions.explain: The on-screen table shows only the most recent 20 entries — investigating anything older requires the downloadable six-month CSV.

questions.prompt: Fill in the blank: if a Policy record is a detail object in a master-detail relationship to Account, its visibility is "________ by Parent" — it automatically follows the Account's access with no separate sharing decision needed per Policy.
questions.explain: Controlled by Parent means the detail record's visibility exactly mirrors its master-detail parent's visibility, which is exactly the 'no separate decision per record' behavior the scenario describes, and is itself a form of implicit sharing.

questions.prompt: Select every true statement about recognizing the right sharing mechanism from an exam-style scenario's wording, per this course's pattern-matching approach.
options: A requirement that says access should apply 'regardless of who owns it' usually points to a criteria-based sharing rule, not an owner-based one
A requirement for temporary, per-deal access that doesn't follow ownership or hierarchy, with membership changing per deal, usually points to a Team
A requirement for access that's dynamically granted when a record enters a status and must be automatically revoked when it leaves that status usually points to Apex managed sharing
A requirement that's 'narrower than the broad grant everyone else gets' usually points to raising the organization-wide default
A requirement that access follow a frequently-changing axis that isn't a management reporting line usually points to Enterprise Territory Management
questions.explain: Criteria-based rules fit ownership-independent requirements; Teams fit per-deal, membership-that-changes-often requirements; Apex managed sharing fits status-conditional grant-and-revoke requirements; territory management fits a frequently-changing, non-hierarchical axis. A 'narrower than everyone else' requirement points to a Restriction Rule, not raising OWD — raising OWD would widen access for everyone, the opposite of what that pattern needs.

questions.prompt: A custom Contract__c object needs every attorney in the Legal public group to get edit access automatically the moment a contract enters Legal Review status, with that access automatically revoked the moment it leaves that status. Which mechanism is the signature fit, and why?
options: A criteria-based sharing rule, because it can express 'while status equals Legal Review' directly

Apex managed sharing, because a trigger or Flow can insert a custom-reason share record on entering the status and explicitly delete it on leaving, which a standard sharing rule can't revoke on its own the same way
Manual sharing, because the access is temporary
A Restriction Rule, because it's the one mechanism that can grant time-limited access
questions.explain: This is status-conditional, dynamically granted and revoked access — the signature use case for Apex managed sharing. A sharing rule can grant based on a status value, but there's no clean declarative way to guarantee the grant disappears automatically and immediately the moment status changes away, the way an explicit Apex-driven delete of the share row does.
